Flat violation rates across F would simply replicate already-published LLM parameter insensitivity (Sticky Collusion, arXiv:2610.39660), not confirm Tsebelis strategic substitution. verdicts.kill_A: Testing Tsebelis's mixed-equilibrium prediction in LLM agents is applying a well-known classical game-theory result to an obvious new domain; LLMs already best-respond to payoff structure (Akata et al., Lorè & Heydari), and the prediction that violations stay flat under F is already foreshadowed by Sticky Collusion (penalty had no significant effect) and Okamoto's penalty paradox, so the cross-dependence may simply reflect known F-insensitivity plus trivial responsiveness to c.
verdicts.kill_B: This is a strict subset of Hypothesis A: it varies only F and predicts violation-rate flatness already suggested by Sticky Collusion and Okamoto et al.; without testing the c dimension it cannot distinguish Tsebelis mixed-equilibrium from simple parameter insensitivity or the already-documented 'fines don't deter LLMs' phenomenon.

verdicts.kill_A: Assumes LLMs converge to mixed Nash equilibria in one-shot games without learning, but models often exhibit direct deterrence sensitivity (F affects violation) or moralizing heuristics (Okamoto arXiv:2608.12323), violating the core insensitivity prediction; the dual cross-dependency requirement doubles the surface area for failure compared to single-variable tests.
verdicts.kill_B: Directly contradicted by prior art (Okamoto et al., Wired Partners) demonstrating fines *do* alter LLM violation rates, making the 'flat violation' prediction empirically fragile; additionally, omitting inspector cost `c` misses the distinctive Tsebelis signature (violator dependence on inspector incentives), reducing mechanistic novelty to a simple null-effect claim.

verdicts.kill_A: The 2x2 factorial still cannot rule out that the LLM merely recites or computes the textbook Tsebelis comparative statics from the displayed payoff numbers (p* depends on c, q* on F) without any genuine strategic interplay between two agents, because the agents never interact and no control removes the game-theoretic prior.
verdicts.kill_B: Only varying F cannot separate the mixed-equilibrium account from the trivial alternative that violators simply ignore penalty size while inspectors relax when fines look large (or when the word 'penalty' is salient): flat violation plus falling inspection is exactly what parameter insensitivity predicts, so no rival explanation is actually excluded.

verdicts.kill_A: The 'single-agent relabelled as swarm' failure mode: with only two agents and a simple payoff matrix, the 'swarm' link is a post-hoc narrative rather than an emergent multi-agent property.
verdicts.kill_B: LLMs often exhibit a 'penalty paradox' or 'fine-as-a-price' effect (Okamoto et al., Wired Partners) where changing F triggers non-game-theoretic behavioral shifts, likely contaminating the violation rate and violating the predicted 'flat' response.

verdicts.kill_A: The distinctive c-prediction demands second-order inference — violators must reason about the inspector's private cost to set p*≈c/(2b) — which one-shot agents of this class are unlikely to exhibit (GTBench; Robinson & Burden's context-dependence critique); if c is hidden from the violator the prediction is incoherent, and if c is printed in the prompt any violation shift is confounded with number salience or prosocial 'don't burden the struggling inspector' framing ...
verdicts.kill_B: The headline 'confirmation' — violation rate flat across F — is exactly what the rival explanation also predicts: LLMs ignoring the penalty number entirely (or sitting at a compliance/violation floor).
